prompt:
Find what the PostgreSQL Global Development Group officially states about how long each major PostgreSQL version receives fixes. Cite the official versioning policy page and quote it.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group officially states that each major version receives fixes for **5 years** from its initial release date.

SOURCE: https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/ | QUOTE: "The PostgreSQL Global Development Group supports a major version for 5 years after its initial release." | CLAIM: Each major PostgreSQL version receives fixes (in the form of minor releases) for 5 years from its initial release date.

---

**Additional context from the same policy:**

SOURCE: https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/ | QUOTE: "After a major version has been released, minor releases will be made available that contain only bug fixes, security fixes, and fixes for data corruption." | CLAIM: During this 5-year support window, the fixes provided are limited to bug fixes, security fixes, and data corruption fixes—no new features are added.

SOURCE: https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/ | QUOTE: "We recommend that all users run the latest available minor release for whatever major version is in use." | CLAIM: Users are expected to apply these minor fix releases promptly, and upgrading between minor versions is considered simpler than major version upgrades.
